newsitem.title: USA: Clinton's inaugural party to be shorter, cheaper.
newsitem.headline: Clinton's inaugural party to be shorter, cheaper.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's second inaugural party will be a day shorter and a few million dollars cheaper than his first, but with one new event that bears the stamp of a loquacious president: public lectures.

The last presidential inauguration this century, indeed this millenium, is scheduled for noon on January 20 when Clinton takes the oath of office for the second time on the west front of the Capitol, home of the U.S. Congress.

That ceremony will be the climax of a three-day celebration. It will be one day shorter than the 1993 ceremony because planners were able to drop a triumphal drive into town by the then-president-elect at the head of a bus caravan.

A new feature this time is a day-long talkathon on January 19 in heated tents on the Washington Mall, the grassy open space running from the Capitol past the White House to the Potomac river where many inaugural events will be held.
Prominent thinkers will lecture on important issues and take questions.

"It's hard to describe in a way that doesn't sound like, 'Oh my God, they're going to talk us to death,'" said Debbie Willhite, the co-executive director of the Presidential Inaugural Committee, which is organising the events.

"But it's much better than that," she said. "Although if we had lectures on all the things that are being talked about we wouldn't finish it in time to get the president's hand on the Bible on Monday."
Among other things, the lectures will focus on "the positive track to the 21st century that President Clinton talked about in his re-election campaign," Willhite said.
"Building a Bridge to the 21st Century," Clinton's oft-repeated campaign slogan, is the inaugural theme and he is likely to refer to it in his second inaugural address.

The theme will also be highlighted during the oath-taking ceremony when a Washington-area children's choir, The Children of the Gospel, sings a song written just for the occasion: "Let's Build a Bridge All Across America."

Opera star Jessye Norman will also sing, as well as Santita Jackson, the daughter of black civil rights leader Jesse Jackson. Arkansas poet Miller Williams will read a poem, and Rev. Billy Graham will give the invocation.
Willhite said the celebration is expected to cost about $30 million, compared to $34.4 million spent in 1993.
The programme begins on January 18 when hundreds of America's top musicians will perform all day on the Mall. That night there will be an enormous fireworks display.
Perhaps in response to questions swirling around recent Democratic campaign fund-raising, the financing of the 1997 inaugural will be more transparent than before.
Officials say there will be full disclosure of the names of all contributors, right down to those who buy a $10 ticket to get a seat for the inaugural parade on Monday afternoon.
No "in-kind" contributions, such as food for parade participants, are being accepted, and contributions will be limited to $100 each.

In 1993, some donations by individuals and corporations were many times that amount. Two of the people at the centre of the campaign fundraising controversy, James Riady and John Huang, jointly gave $100,000 to Clinton's 1993 inaugural.
Inaugural financing enjoyed a head start this time around with $9 million that was left over from four years ago.

More cash will be raised at an invitation-only presidential gala on January 19 at the U.S. Air Arena, a major sports and entertainment centre. It is expected to be attended by some 14,000 people paying between $100 and $3,000 a ticket.
Organisers hoped to raise another $500,000 from selling souvenirs like T-shirts and mugs.
Then there are the 12 inaugural balls, which may be attended by as many as 70,000 people paying up to $150 each.

The inaugural ceremony itself and the parade are free and open to the public on a standing-room basis. But to sit down at either event one needs tickets that will be issued on an invitation-only basis.
